item.title: The Quiet Beginning of Trust
item.description:
Trust

The Quiet Beginning of Trust

Why we feel safe with some people instantly.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • Trust often begins before words are exchanged.
  • Signals of presence shape whether we feel safe.
  • Attention may be one of the most powerful forms of care.
Presence is the quality of our attention
Source: StockPlanets / iStock

For many years, there was something about clinical practice that puzzled me.

Two physicians could meet patients with similar expertise, similar experience, and equally sincere intentions, yet leave remarkably different impressions. Both listened carefully, both explained diagnoses clearly, and both prescribed appropriate treatment. Yet one consultation somehow seemed to settle the person sitting opposite, while another—despite being entirely competent—left a trace of uncertainty that neither doctor nor patient could quite explain.

Early in my career I assumed this difference reflected communication skills. Perhaps one clinician explained things more clearly or appeared more confident. Maybe experience simply taught us how to reassure people more effectively.

Over time, however, I became less certain. The difference often seemed to emerge before very much had been said at all. It was there in the first moments of entering the room. If you were observant, you might notice the quality of a greeting, a glance, or the pace at which someone sat down. You could sense whether attention seemed divided or completely available. These moments were so brief that they were easy to overlook, yet they often appeared to influence everything that followed.

Medicine has traditionally placed enormous emphasis on what clinicians know and what they say. Both matter greatly. Competence saves lives, and clear communication remains one of the foundations of good care. Yet after many years of seeing patients, I have come to believe that something equally important happens before either knowledge or language can fully do their work: Trust has already begun to form. This is not simply an intuition; psychology has gradually caught up with what many experienced clinicians have long suspected.

Several decades ago, psychologist Nalini Ambady demonstrated that people form remarkably accurate impressions of others from what she called "thin slices" of behavior. Watching only a few seconds of silent video was often enough for observers to make judgments that closely matched the impressions of people who had known those individuals for much longer. We appear to notice far more than we consciously realize.

Most of us imagine ourselves making careful, rational assessments of other people. Our minds are constantly gathering information beneath conscious awareness. Facial expression, posture, tone of voice, timing, movement, and attention all contribute to a rapid sense of whether another person feels trustworthy, interested, or emotionally present. These impressions are rarely infallible, but neither are they random. They represent one of the ways human beings have learned to navigate relationships throughout our evolutionary history.

More recently, Stephen Porges' work has helped illuminate why these first moments matter so profoundly. Long before we consciously analyze a conversation, our nervous system is already searching for signs of safety. We respond not only to words but also to qualities of voice, facial expression, eye contact, and the subtle rhythm of human interaction. Much of this happens automatically, outside conscious awareness.

When those signals suggest calmness, openness, and genuine availability, something within us begins to settle. We become more able to think clearly, ask difficult questions, absorb information, and speak honestly about our concerns. When those signals are absent, even excellent information may struggle to find fertile ground. This helps explain something every clinician has experienced. Patients occasionally tell us that they "just felt listened to," even when the consultation itself was relatively brief. Others may leave with detailed explanations yet remain uneasy, despite receiving objectively good care.

The difference is not usually charisma, nor is it personality. More often, it reflects whether another human being experienced us as being fully present. Presence is a deceptively simple word. It is sometimes mistaken for a communication technique or another professional competency that can be added to an already crowded curriculum. My own experience has led me to see it differently.

Presence is not something we perform; it is the quality of attention we bring into the encounter itself.

Patients are remarkably sensitive to whether our attention has already moved to the next appointment, the next task, or the next problem waiting outside the consultation room. Equally, they notice when, even briefly, they have become the only person who exists in that moment. Ironically, such presence often requires no additional time. It asks instead for a different way of arriving.

The same principle extends well beyond individual consultations. Amy Edmondson's work on psychological safety has shown that the highest-performing teams are not necessarily those with the greatest technical expertise. They are the teams in which people feel sufficiently safe to ask questions, acknowledge uncertainty, and admit mistakes without fear of humiliation or blame. Learning becomes possible because safety already exists.

Healthcare depends precisely on this kind of environment. Every member of a clinical team must be able to raise concerns, question assumptions, and share incomplete information when patient safety depends upon it. Knowledge certainly matters, but knowledge alone cannot create openness. People speak more honestly when they sense that they will be received with respect.

Whether we are caring for patients, leading teams, or teaching students, the same principle consistently reappears. Before people decide whether to believe our advice, they are often deciding whether they feel safe in our company. This places presence at the very heart of healthcare—not as an optional refinement but as one of the conditions that allows expertise to be received. Information rarely changes people unless safety has first created space for it to land.

Looking back across many years of medicine, I no longer think the opening moments of a consultation are simply an introduction before the real work begins. They are already part of the work. Long before symptoms are explored, diagnoses considered or treatments discussed, two human beings are already exchanging something far more fundamental.

Without saying very much at all, each is asking the other a quiet question:

Am I safe with you?

item.title: The Eyes of Criminals Often Tell the Rest of the Story
item.description:
Deception

The Eyes of Criminals Often Tell the Rest of the Story

From the bench: When someone lies, that deception is reflected in their eyes.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • A criminal's eyes can frequently reveal whether or not they feel genuine remorse.
  • Our pupils and involuntary micro-expressions naturally give away our true hidden feelings.
  • If a convicted criminal shows true remorse, there is a chance they can be successfully rehabilitated.

Over the years, I saw thousands of juvenile defendants come through my courtroom, ranging from 10 to 17 years old. Some appeared for minor infractions, such as violating the city curfew, while others faced transfers to adult court for severe crimes like aggravated assault and murder. Regardless of the charges, I learned that a defendant's eyes always revealed one of three distinct stories—even if I had to instruct them to look up at me instead of staring at the floor. They were either terrified youths who had made a genuine mistake, individuals driven to crime by the unrelenting pressures of their environment who still possessed a capacity for remorse, or hardened individuals—whether due to severe mental health issues or cold-blooded calculation—who would just as soon murder me if given the chance, showing absolutely no remorse or potential for rehabilitation.

Pupils Reveal Emotions and Intentions

In a post for Psychology Today, David Ludden, Ph.D., explores a theory espoused by psychologists Sebastiaan Mathôt and Stefan Van der Stigchel in Current Directions in Psychological Science. They argue that there is much more to the pupillary light response than meets the eye, claiming that pupil size reveals a wealth of information about a person's underlying emotions and intentions. Ludden notes that light is not the only factor affecting pupil size; our pupils also dilate when we become aroused. The autonomic nervous system acts as the body's alarm network, preparing us to take immediate action whenever we detect either a threat or an opportunity in our surroundings.

When someone lies, that deception is directly reflected in their eyes. Scientific research supports the idea that deceit is revealed not by the direction of a person's gaze but by the changing size of their pupils. Deception causes the pupillary diameter to expand, an involuntary reaction that occurs even if it remains invisible to the naked eye.

How Micro-Expressions Reveal True Emotions

Beyond pupil dilation, other ocular behaviors justify calling the eyes the "window to the soul." Micro-expressions—involuntary facial movements that flash across a person's face for a mere fraction of a second—reveal authentic emotions before the brain has time to conceal them. The primary zone for detecting these hidden feelings is the eyes and the immediate surrounding area. When a person feels fear, their lower eyelids tense and pull slightly inward. When surprised, their eyes widen as their jaw drops. In moments of anger, the muscles around the eye sockets instantly tighten. Furthermore, a genuine smile can be distinguished from a fake one by the presence of crow's feet, caused by the contraction of muscles at the outer corners of the eyes. A fake smile moves the mouth while leaving the eyes flat, cold, and unwrinkled.

As we navigate our daily lives across professional, personal, private, and public spheres, we should learn to trust the eyes and trust our instincts. The next time you observe a convicted criminal defendant, look closely at their eyes to see if you can spot genuine remorse. If you find it, then maybe, just maybe, they can still be rehabilitated.

item.title: Americans Rate Nation's Moral Values at All-Time Low
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Americans Rate Nation's Moral Values at All-Time Low

People often rate their own virtues highly but worry about everyone else.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • Americans report that moral values are at an all-time low.
  • Maybe they are pointing to social conventions, not morality.
  • Morality can be judged by a universal standard.

Americans think that the nation’s moral values are in trouble, with more than half in a recent Gallup poll rating them as poor and 80% as getting worse. In fact, this is the lowest rating since Gallup began polling around this question in 2002.

Not surprisingly, it is the other guy’s moral compass that is considered broken. Democrats point the finger at Republicans and Republicans point to Democrats as moral failures, while the non-committed think both sides stink.

This strikes me like the findings around how people rate their own driving: up to 80% say they are above average drivers.

Driving statistics can be a fair proxy for ethical behavior if you understand morality as taking another’s interest into account. Confirming everyday observations, driving has gotten worse in recent years, with increased drunk and distracted driving, road rage, the disregard for stop signs and turn signals, and excessive speeding.

Subjectivity in Moral Judgments

What counts as moral also can be in the eye of the beholder, as illustrated by the irate Long Islander who complained about beaches and parks that allow “the public display of rear nudity.” The display of buttocks in skimpy bathing suits not only flouts community standards, the letter-writer says, but more importantly it feeds into a hyper-sexualized culture that “ultimately degrades societal values.”

Imperiling the lives of others while driving and offending others with attire (or lack thereof) at the beach point to a difficulty with many discussions about morality. Both can be defined as moral issues, but there is a distinction between them. Putting others at risk is a universal concern, while what is acceptable dress is a social convention. Think of the more than 2,000-year-old Hippocratic Oath, which admonishes physicians to do no harm while written by men in tunics.

Decent people understand it is wrong to gratuitously harm another while reasonable people can disagree about which body parts can be exposed under what circumstances.

The Newsday writer does make a point worth considering, though. Social conventions are often considered moral matters because they relate to an important part of living with others. They help bond people by sorting through who may be trusted. When someone disregards social mores, you rightfully become skeptical and wonder if they are also inclined to more consequential misbehavior.

How Moral Rules and Social Conventions Evolve Over Time

At the same time, moral rules, such as regulating attire, differ from time to time and from culture to culture. When I was a teenager, for example, wearing a shirt in the park was mandatory even while playing basketball in the heat of summer. Today, in New York, women are legally permitted to be topless wherever it is acceptable for men to be bare-chested.

Morality, at the level of social convention, means that another way to behave could be chosen that is also beneficial to social living. Using cutlery is a social convention, as is looking a person in the eye when being chastised. In some places, chopsticks are used when eating and looking someone in the eye who is your elder is disrespectful. These are amongst the myriad practices that define a culture.

There will always be disagreements regarding the application of ethical values. Some cultures stress one above another, individuals’ temperaments differ, and cultures respond to unique environmental conditions and historic developments. Still, morality can be judged against a universal standard. Those practices that enhance the human spirit are good and right; those practices that degrade human dignity and disrespect people are bad and wrong. Looking at ethical traditions from around the world, we find these ethical values stand out: benevolence, compassion, lovingkindness, respect, truth-telling, humility, and fairness.

Beyond doubt, however, these virtues make life worthwhile, a moral compass that is personal and social at the same time.

item.title: Why “Closure” Is a Fairy Tale
item.description:
Grief

Why “Closure” Is a Fairy Tale

Our culture often treats grief and negative feelings like dirty words.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • We live in a "be strong and move on" society that prioritizes joy while shunning negative emotions.
  • Closure implies that we should sever our bonds with the past and diminish the importance of what we’ve lost.
  • Viewing grief as an involuntary beginning can allow us to dignify our suffering.

When we face profound loss and adversity—the death of a loved one, financial hardship, illness, or the end of a relationship—the concept of "closure" is often presented as the ultimate goal. We are pressured to follow a rigid protocol, as if healing were a linear path toward a final destination where our pain simply evaporates. Society expects us to "get over it," but human attachment isn't something that can be easily dismantled or forgotten.

The demand for closure can feel both impossible and insulting. It implies that we should sever our bonds with the past or diminish the importance of what we’ve lost. Closure suggests a single moment where grief stops, rather than a lifelong journey of integration. It rushes the process, telling us to "let go" and focus on the living, which can lead to suppressed emotions rather than genuine healing. The memories and love we hold for those we've lost are permanent; they don't have an expiration date.

True healing isn't about the "grit" required to move on quickly. Instead, it is the transformative process of converting pain into a new way of existing. Rushing toward an arbitrary finish line can actually increase our suffering and hinder our ability to live authentically with our experiences. Taking the time to mourn and process grief is as essential to the human experience as love and laughter. This process has no timeline, no rules, and no fixed protocol.

As author Marisa Renee Lee notes, “Grief is the repeated experience of learning to live in the midst of a significant loss.” Ultimately, thriving isn't found by closing a door on the past, but by learning to carry our history with us as we build a meaningful future.

Our Culture’s Response to Grief

We live in a "be strong and move on" society that prioritizes joy while shunning negative emotions. This cultural pressure often forces us to rush the grieving process, dismissing long-term sorrow as a sign of weakness. We are told to "let go" and "stop living in the past," leaving many to mourn in isolation.

Ironically, our bodies are biologically wired for both laughter and tears. While laughter releases endorphins, crying releases oxytocin and natural opioids that serve as internal painkillers. Suppressing these tears is physically and emotionally counterproductive; mourning is as vital to being alive as breathing oxygen.

Though our culture often veils grief in shame, the irony is that leaning into it is the true elixir for healing. By banishing grief, we reject the very tool we need most to thrive.

Seeking Comfort Over Closure

In 2014, while covering the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines flight MH370, CNN journalist Anderson Cooper interviewed a grief counselor working with the victims' families. When asked how he helped these families reach "closure," the psychologist countered that closure is a damaging concept after such profound tragedy. He argued that there is no tidy ending; instead, the most effective support is simple human comfort—offering presence without trying to "fix" the unfixable or follow a rigid psychological script.

Grieving is not a path toward a finish line, but a process of teaching the heart and soul to coexist with wounds that never truly heal. Grief functions like a permanent scar; while it may fade over the decades, the mark remains visible for a lifetime. It is a part of our anatomy that we carry forward, rather than a chapter we eventually close.

When I lost both of my parents in 2004, the impact was devastating. Even now, over 20 years later, the ache persists. I find comfort not by moving on, but by surrounding myself with their photos—images of them healthy and joyful. Looking back is often like running my fingers over a sensitive scar; it can be painful, but I do it because living with that sadness is more honest than trying to erase it. We must learn to hold our pain in high regard rather than viewing it as something to be discarded.

Viewing grief as an involuntary beginning allows us to dignify our suffering. It requires us to live with the reality of not forgetting, accepting that owning a human heart comes with the liability of being permanently scarred. Yet, these scars possess a unique resilience. They prepare us for life’s future inevitabilities and deepen our appreciation for the present, fostering a more compassionate and aesthetic mindset that finds meaning in everyday depth. Hence, grief teaches how to live better.

As Marcel Proust observed, "Happiness is beneficial for the body, but it is grief that develops the powers of the mind." By acknowledging our scars, we find the magic in the tragic—the realization that we can endure despite the pain and convert pain into purpose. We ultimately yield to the finite nature of our existence: we are born, we form deep attachments, we love fiercely, and eventually, we must say goodbye. It’s not about liking this reality. It’s about honoring it.
